lesson.title: Private Attributes: Python's Honor-System Privacy
lesson.summary: Python has no attribute access that the interpreter truly forbids; instead it offers naming conventions, a single leading underscore to mean "internal use, please don't touch," and a double leading underscore to trigger name mangling that makes accidental outside access harder, though never impossible.
lesson.body:
The Thermostat example ended on an uncomfortable truth: nothing stopped code outside the class from setting t.temperature directly and skipping the validation in set_temperature entirely. Some languages solve this with a private keyword that the compiler genuinely enforces. Python takes a different approach, one that's important to describe accurately rather than oversell. Building on the instance attributes you already know how to create in __init__, and on the encapsulation goal from the last chapter of steering interaction through methods, Python offers two naming conventions instead of a hard lock.

A single leading underscore, like self._id, is a signal to other programmers: "this attribute is for internal use inside the class, please don't rely on it or set it directly from outside." Python does absolutely nothing to enforce this. It's a convention, respected by tooling and other developers, but code outside the class can still read or write self._id without any error at all.

A double leading underscore, like self.__balance, does something more: Python performs name mangling. Any identifier written with two leading underscores (and at most one trailing underscore) that appears textually inside a class body gets automatically rewritten by the interpreter to _ClassName__attributename. So self.__balance, written inside class Wallet, is actually stored as self._Wallet__balance. This doesn't make the attribute inaccessible, but it does mean code outside the class can't accidentally collide with it or casually type wallet.__balance and expect it to work.

```python
class Wallet:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.__balance = balance

w = Wallet(100)
print(w._Wallet__balance)
# Output: 100

try:
    print(w.__balance)
except AttributeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)
# Output: Error: 'Wallet' object has no attribute '__balance'
# (the exact wording can vary slightly between Python versions)
```

Trace through why both lines behave the way they do. Inside __init__, the line self.__balance = balance is textually inside the Wallet class body, so Python mangles it at compile time into self._Wallet__balance = balance, meaning the real attribute name stored on the object is _Wallet__balance, holding 100. The line print(w._Wallet__balance), typed out here at the module level using that full mangled name directly, works fine and prints 100, because that genuinely is the attribute's real name; mangling doesn't hide it, it just renames it. But w.__balance, also typed at the module level, is not inside any class body, so Python does not mangle it, it looks for an attribute literally named __balance, which was never created, so it raises an AttributeError. This is exactly why double underscore is described as making access harder rather than impossible: the mangled name is still discoverable and still directly accessible if you know it, it's just no longer the obvious, guessable name.
